issues.legal_issue: When returned income falls below the prescribed proportion of assessed income, the resulting presumption of concealment remains operative unless the taxpayer rebuts it with cogent, relevant material.
material_facts: The taxpayer’s returned income was below the threshold specified in the applicable Explanation to the concealment-penalty provision.
An unexplained payment made for a property investment was treated as undisclosed income after the taxpayer could not establish its nature and source.
The Tribunal accepted that the taxpayer’s explanation of available cash was not merely unconvincing but false, and that no explanation had been given for the source of the extra payment.
No cogent, reliable and relevant material was identified as rebutting the presumption.
issues.conclusion: The presumption that concealment resulted from fraud or gross or wilful neglect remained unrebutted; the Tribunal was not justified in cancelling the penalty on the reasoning it adopted.
issues.legal_principle: Under the Explanation to section 271(1)(c) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, as introduced by the Finance Act, 1964, where returned income was less than 80 per cent of the assessed income as adjusted under the Explanation, the taxpayer was presumed to have concealed income unless the taxpayer proved that the failure to return correct income did not arise from fraud or gross or wilful neglect. The presumption was rebuttable, but rebuttal required relevant and cogent material, whose relevance and sufficiency were for the fact-finding body to assess. The Court applied C.I.T. v. Mussadilal Ram Bharose and distinguished the approach associated with C.I.T. v. Anwar Ali and C.I.T. v. Khoday Ramarao & Sons, on which the Tribunal had relied.

rule.if: penalty_concealment_proceeding and returned_income_below_threshold and unexplained_investment_treated_as_income and explanation_found_false and not cogent_rebuttal_material

predicates.penalty_concealment_proceeding: A penalty proceeding alleges concealment of income or furnishing inaccurate income particulars.
predicates.returned_income_below_threshold: The taxpayer’s returned income is below the prescribed proportion of the income assessed, after applicable adjustments.
predicates.unexplained_investment_treated_as_income: The taxpayer cannot establish the nature and source of funds used for an investment, and the amount is treated as income.
predicates.explanation_found_false: The fact-finding body finds that the taxpayer’s explanation for the source of the funds is false.
predicates.cogent_rebuttal_material: The taxpayer produces cogent, reliable and relevant material rebutting the presumption of concealment.

issues.definition: When a concealment-penalty proceeding involves returned income below the threshold and unexplained investment treated as income, a false explanation and the absence of cogent rebuttal material mean that the concealment presumption remains unrebutted.

issues.legal_issue: A refusal to require a reference cannot stand when the tribunal’s cancellation of a concealment penalty rests on an incorrect application of the governing presumption and raises a legal question.
material_facts: The Tribunal cancelled the penalty even though it accepted that the taxpayer’s explanation was false and identified no cogent material rebutting the presumption.
The Tribunal refused to refer the Revenue’s questions of law, and the High Court also held that no question of law arose.
The Supreme Court held that the High Court had failed to apply the principles in C.I.T. v. Mussadilal Ram Bharose correctly and directed that a statement of the case be sent to the High Court.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s refusal was set aside, and the Tribunal was directed to forward a statement of the case to the High Court for determination of the referred question of law.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 256(2) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, a reference is warranted where the Tribunal’s decision presents a question of law. The Court held that the Tribunal’s treatment of the rebuttable presumption, contrary to C.I.T. v. Mussadilal Ram Bharose, raised such a question; the High Court’s refusal to direct a reference was therefore erroneous.

rule.if: reference_proceeding_after_tribunal_order and tribunal_cancelled_penalty_despite_false_explanation and not cogent_rebuttal_material and high_court_refused_reference

predicates.reference_proceeding_after_tribunal_orde: A party seeks a reference to the High Court after the Tribunal has refused to refer a question arising from its order.
predicates.tribunal_cancelled_penalty_despite_false: The Tribunal cancels a concealment penalty even though it accepts that the taxpayer’s explanation is false.
predicates.cogent_rebuttal_material: The taxpayer produces cogent, reliable and relevant material rebutting the presumption of concealment.
predicates.high_court_refused_reference: The High Court declines to require the Tribunal to state the case for reference.

issues.definition: In a reference proceeding after a Tribunal order, if the Tribunal cancels a penalty despite a false explanation and there is no cogent rebuttal material, the High Court’s refusal requires the case to be referred to it.
